Hard · Mobility and logistics

Ride-hailing dispatch

You run dispatch for a big metro area. About 100,000 drivers send a position every 4 seconds, and riders ask for cars near them. When a stadium empties, thousands of riders ask for a car from the same few blocks at the same moment. Match riders to drivers fast, and never charge a trip twice. Practise this hard system design problem for free with a Google or GitHub account.

Play this problem

The brief

You run dispatch for a big metro area. About 100,000 drivers send a position every 4 seconds, and riders ask for cars near them. When a stadium empties, thousands of riders ask for a car from the same few blocks at the same moment. Match riders to drivers fast, and never charge a trip twice.

Think of an app like Uber.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
15 million riders and 600,000 drivers a month, 100,000 drivers online at peak (approx.)
Audience in plain numbers
15,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 30,000 requests per second
Request mix
Location ping: 80%; Read: 12%; Write: 4%; Payment: 0.5%; Notification: 3.5%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 300 ms; Write: ≈ 300 ms; Payment: ≈ 3,000 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $40,000
Data at rest
≈ 2 TB
Where users are
North America: 100%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Location ping: 900 seconds; Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Payment: 3,600 seconds; Notification: 900 seconds
Fresh reads
People must see their own changes. At most 0.1% of reads may be stale in the model.
Personal reads
80% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.
Required proofs
Managed encryption keys; Personal data isolated

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • 100,000 drivers x one ping per 4 s is about 25,000 pings a second. Locations are 80 percent of traffic.
  • Rider reads are nearby-car lookups and price quotes. Writes are ride state changes: request, accept, start, end.
  • All numbers are rough approximations.
  • Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

Questions that shape the design

How accurate must the car positions be?

A rider sees cars that are a few seconds old. Dispatch itself needs the freshest position of each driver.

What happens at a stadium exit?

Thousands of requests come from one small area in a few minutes. One map cell can get a third of all lookups.

Can a ride request be lost?

No. Once a rider is told a car is coming, the trip record must survive a server failure.

Is a duplicate charge ever acceptable?

Never. A trip is charged once, even if the network retries.

The traffic day

Morning and evening commute peaks. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 08:10 · Zone outage

    An availability zone loses power or network access.

    Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

  2. 17:45 · Hot key

    One item gets a huge share of traffic: a celebrity profile, one product, one merchant.

    Affected share: 30%. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

  3. 22:45 · Flash crowd

    A scheduled launch brings a sudden rush of requests.

    Traffic for Read, Write, Notification reaches 6 times the scheduled load; rises over 60 seconds, holds for 1,800 seconds and eases over 1,800 seconds. Other request types keep their scheduled load.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Location pings are four out of five requests and each one is tiny. Do they belong in the same database as ride records?
  • Claim a driver once despite stale locations and concurrent matching.
  • Reading a position back with consistency level ONE is fast and can be a few seconds stale. A driver position is stale after 4 seconds anyway.
  • A 5 second cache means a rider can see a car that just took another trip. The match step re-checks with the driver before it commits.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Related problems

    Battle royale launch

    On launch night millions of players queue for matches of 100. Each match streams positions many times a second, the lobby shows the live player count, and one patch notes page is opened by everyone. Connections must stay open, a match server dying must preserve acknowledged progress within the stated recovery point, and a few hot items, like the daily reward, are hit by everybody.

  • Medium

    Food delivery

    You run food delivery in a few big cities. People browse menus, pay for an order, and watch a courier move on a map. Dinner time is brutal, and the payment company sometimes slows down. Nobody may be charged twice, and no paid order may vanish.

  • Medium

    Rate limiter for a public API

    Developers call your public API from scripts and apps. A few misbehaving or malicious clients can crowd out everyone else. Build limits that are fair, fast and cheap, and that survive a retry storm.

  • Hard

    Object storage service

    Customers store billions of files, from tiny pictures to huge videos, and fetch them by name. The service must never lose a file, scale without a limit and stay cheap. Most files are written once and rarely read again.
